--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.maximum_spanning_tree()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Find the maximum spanning tree using Kruskal's algorithm. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.maximum_spanning_tree()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Find the maximum spanning tree using Kruskal's algorithm. title: >- [Graph.maximum_spanning_tree()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Find the maximum spanning tree using Kruskal's algorithm. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find the maximum spanning tree using Kruskal's algorithm. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L80363-L80497){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.maximum_spanning_tree( weight_attr=None, return_subgraph=True, include=None, exclude=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Maximum spanning tree](../assets/graphs/maximum-spanning-tree.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same weighted graph as the minimum spanning tree figure. The maximum spanning tree keeps the heaviest edges that still form a tree: D–E (7), B–E (6), A–D (5), and C–D (3), in the accent color. The card lists them and their total weight, 7 + 6 + 5 + 3 = 21." width="100%"} A maximum spanning tree is a subset of edges that connects all nodes with the maximum total edge weight, without forming any cycle. It is computed exactly like `minimum_spanning_tree()`, except that Kruskal's algorithm considers the edges from heaviest to lightest, keeping each edge that joins two not-yet-connected parts of the tree. When edge weights measure *strength* (similarity, interaction frequency, bandwidth, correlation) rather than cost, the maximum spanning tree keeps the strongest possible set of links that still reaches every node. Common uses include: - extracting the backbone of a dense similarity or correlation network - finding the highest-capacity routes that connect every site (the path between two nodes in the tree maximizes its weakest link) - building tree-structured models from pairwise scores, such as Chow-Liu trees Edge direction is ignored, so on a directed graph the result is a spanning tree of the underlying undirected graph (the chosen edges keep their original orientation). If the graph is disconnected, the result is a maximum spanning *forest*: one tree per connected component. Self-loops are never selected. The original graph is not modified. With `include=` and `exclude=`, the tree is the heaviest one that uses every included edge and none of the excluded ones (NetworkX's `partition_spanning_tree()` with `minimum=False`). ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute to use as the weight. If `None` (the default), each edge's weight field is used (edges on an unweighted graph count as `1.0`, so any spanning tree is maximal). If a name is given, every edge must hold a number under it; `"weight"` names the weight field. [return_subgraph]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (the default), returns a new `Graph` containing every node of the original graph and only the tree edges. If `False`, returns the selected edges as `(source_id, target_id, weight)` tuples in the order Kruskal's algorithm picked them, from heaviest to lightest (included edges first). [include]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Edges the tree must contain, as edge IDs or `(u, v)` node pairs (a pair stands for every edge between the two nodes, in either direction). They must not form a cycle. [exclude]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Edges the tree must not contain, given the same way. Excluding edges can disconnect the graph, in which case the result is a spanning forest. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph or list[tuple[int, int, float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_subgraph=` is `True`: a new `Graph` with the same directedness and weighting, every node of the original (same IDs, labels and attributes) and the tree edges (same IDs, weights and attributes). If `return_subgraph=` is `False`: a list of `(source_id, target_id, weight)` tuples, the weight being the value the tree was built with (the `weight_attr=` attribute when one is named). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the included edges contain a cycle, an edge is both included and excluded, an edge or node pair in `include=`/`exclude=` does not exist, (with constraints) an edge value is NaN, or `weight_attr=` names an attribute that an edge lacks or holds as a non-number. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Same Kruskal pipeline as `minimum_spanning_tree()` with the weight comparator reversed (equivalently, running MST on $-w$), so cost is $O(E \log E)$ and correctness follows from the cut and cycle properties applied to the negated weights. The construction is a standard tool for extracting a network *backbone*: retain the strongest relationships in a social graph, the highest-throughput links in a communication network, or the most similar species in a hierarchical clustering. Behaves exactly like the minimum variant on disconnected input, yielding one maximum spanning tree per component. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~minimum_spanning_tree`) : The tree with the smallest total weight. [](`~iter_spanning_trees`) : The spanning trees in order of weight, with `minimum=False`. [](`~maximum_spanning_arborescence`) : The heaviest spanning tree that follows edge directions. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a graph whose weights measure how strong a link is, the maximum spanning tree keeps the strongest links that don't close a cycle. In this square, the weakest edge is left out: ::: {#c9b92df4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B", 4.0), ("B", "C", 3.0), ("C", "D", 2.0), ("D", "A", 1.0)], ) graph.maximum_spanning_tree().get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['A--B', 'B--C', 'C--D'] ``` ::: ::: ### The backbone of a novel `les_miserables()` links two characters of Victor Hugo's novel when they appear in the same chapter, weighted by how many chapters they share. Of its 254 links, the maximum spanning tree keeps the 76 strongest that still tie all 77 characters together. Its strongest link is between Cosette and Valjean, who share 31 chapters: ::: {#6bccf839 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} novel = ec.les_miserables() backbone = novel.maximum_spanning_tree() edges = backbone.get_edge_df().sort("weight", descending=True) label = backbone.get_label_from_id top = edges.row(0, named=True) backbone.count_edges(), label(top["source"]), label(top["target"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (76, 'Cosette', 'Valjean') ``` ::: ::: The backbone hangs from Valjean, who keeps 17 of 36 links in it: ::: {#f83566bc .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} backbone.layout_spring(seed=1).plot( layout="pos", size_by="degree", label_by="label", height=600 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
